This also gives an instant rollback by swapping back. An immutable update (C) launches new instances and moves traffic once health checks pass, but there is no separate stage to test the new code before customers hit it, and immutable updates cannot move to a different platform branch. A unit test therefore just builds a sample SQS event (for example with sam local generate-event sqs receive-message or a JSON fixture) and calls the handler in the test framework, checking the result; this is fast, isolated and runs in CI without AWS resources. Creating a real test queue (C) or deploying a stack and invoking the deployed function (A) are integration tests that depend on live AWS infrastructure. Running aws lambda invoke against a deployed function (D) is also not a unit test. Option B's wording is awkward, but it is the only one built on a test event.

An SQS FIFO queue with message deduplication IDs gives exactly-once processing and the extra request cost is small, so it is the most direct fix among the options (in practice you create a new FIFO queue, since an existing queue cannot be converted). Setting Lambda concurrency to 1 severely limits throughput and still allows redelivery after a visibility timeout, and SQS event source mappings require a maximum concurrency of at least 2. A dead-letter queue only captures failed messages, and Kinesis Data Streams also delivers at least once. The best real-world fixes are a visibility timeout of at least six times the function timeout plus idempotent processing.

Using the S3 static website endpoint requires a public bucket policy because website endpoints do not support OAC, which breaks the requirement. A custom 404 error response returning /index.html would serve the root page for every missing path instead of each directory's own index page.

Combined with the function's CloudWatch Logs, which Lambda writes automatically, this is the lowest-overhead way to find the cause. Raising the Lambda timeout to 15 minutes and checking CloudTrail does not help, because CloudTrail does not log function errors. A DynamoDB table requires custom code. Increasing the visibility timeout is good practice for timeouts but does not by itself capture failed messages.

Option D describes console test events, which only run functions deployed in AWS, not on a local machine. Option B's aws lambda invoke calls the deployed cloud function. Option A uploads a real object, and S3 cannot invoke a function on a developer's machine.

If errors appear, setting the weight back to 0% for the new version rolls back instantly, and only a tenth of users ever saw the problem, which minimizes impact. Option A also allows rollback by repointing the alias, but every user hits the new version first. Option C needs an application change to roll back, and option D is invalid because an alias cannot point to another alias.

saa-0580.note: The key says A (geolocation), but the goal is to minimize load time, and latency-based routing (C) is built for that. Geolocation routes by where the user is located, not by measured network latency, and needs a default record for users outside the defined areas.

For the on-premises data center, you create a latency record tagged with the us-west-1 Region because the data center is near it, and a second record for the eu-central-1 endpoint. Geolocation routing sends users to an endpoint based on country or continent, which often matches latency but is not optimized for it, and users outside the listed locations need a default record. Simple routing cannot pick an endpoint based on user location at all. Weighted routing splits traffic evenly no matter where users are. Option C's wording is incomplete, so this question is debatable, but latency routing best fits the stated goal.

S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval is not readily available because retrievals take minutes to hours. Starting in Intelligent-Tiering and then adding a lifecycle rule to Standard-IA is redundant and adds monitoring charges.

Shorter duration often offsets the higher per-millisecond price, which cuts compute cost while keeping latency down. Reserved concurrency costs nothing and guarantees that this function always has its share of account concurrency available during marketing events, so other functions cannot starve it. Provisioned concurrency keeps environments warm but is billed continuously, which conflicts with reducing cost for spiky event traffic. Decreasing memory would slow CPU-bound code and increase latency.

It works for any TCP protocol, so RTMP needs no change. CloudFront is a content delivery network for HTTP and HTTPS delivery to viewers; it does not proxy RTMP ingest, and its old RTMP distributions served only playback and have been retired. Client VPN adds encryption and overhead without acceleration. EC2 instances with Elastic IPs give static addresses but no network acceleration.

saa-0844.note: I believe the answer is B. A recurring scheduled action is the Auto Scaling feature built for predictable, recurring peaks and adds capacity before the spike; option C (raising min/max during the peak) is a manual, after-the-fact step.

Scheduling the increase ahead of the known peak means instances are already running and warm when traffic arrives, which is exactly what proactive scaling means. A CloudWatch alarm on 90% CPU is reactive and scales only after users are already affected. Raising min and max 'during the peak demand period' is manual and happens too late unless someone remembers to do it in advance. An SNS notification on instance launch only alerts and does not add capacity.

saa-0876.note: The keyed answer (centralized mailbox for root emails plus one distribution list per category) is defensible, but option B (company-managed distribution lists per business unit) is also a commonly argued answer; both avoid tying root email to an individual.

AWS account alternate contacts let billing, operations and security notifications go to separate addresses, so business-managed distribution lists per category send each notification type to the right team. Option C ties the root email to one person, which is a single point of failure and a security risk. Option A gives every account owner access to the shared root mailbox, widening access to root credentials. Option B is close, but distribution lists that fan out to many administrators expose root-level emails to more people.

Sending purchase requests to an SQS queue decouples the front end from processing, so requests are never lost and an Auto Scaling group of workers drains the queue at a sustainable rate. Amazon RDS Proxy pools and reuses database connections, which protects Aurora from connection storms as the worker fleet scales. ElastiCache mostly helps read-heavy workloads, while purchases are writes. A Lambda retry loop does not add capacity, and an API Gateway usage plan only throttles clients.

saa-0890.note: A single-instance Auto Scaling group (A) is the classic 'self-healing legacy app' answer, but two instances behind an NLB (C) is also argued; it depends on whether the legacy app can safely run as two copies.
saa-0890.aiExplanation: Because the application design cannot change, it may not be able to run as multiple active copies. An Auto Scaling group with minimum and maximum of one, spanning multiple Availability Zones, built from an AMI of the server, automatically replaces the instance in another AZ if it or its AZ fails, and a load balancer in front gives a stable endpoint. Running two copies behind an NLB (C) assumes the app can run in parallel, which a legacy design may not support. Hourly backups with manual restore give slow recovery and can lose up to an hour of data. Refactoring into containers violates the no-design-change constraint.

saa-0916.note: I believe the answer is A. With millions of 10 KB files, S3 Standard-IA bills each object as at least 128 KB, and S3 Lifecycle by default does not transition objects under 128 KB, so aggregating files into large objects is the cost-effective approach.
saa-0916.aiExplanation: With millions of tiny 10 KB files, per-object overheads dominate cost: S3 Standard-IA and Glacier Instant Retrieval charge a 128 KB minimum per object, lifecycle transitions are charged per request, and Glacier Deep Archive adds about 40 KB of metadata overhead per object. S3 Lifecycle also skips objects smaller than 128 KB by default. Bundling the files into large archive objects before uploading with DataSync removes almost all of that overhead. Glacier Instant Retrieval still gives millisecond access for the rare reads in year one, and a lifecycle rule moves the archives to Glacier Deep Archive for the 7-year retention. Option D stores each 10 KB file as its own object, which is billed as 128 KB in Standard-IA and needs millions of transitions. Options B and C keep data in more expensive tiers for the 7-year archive.

saa-0920.note: I believe B. Assigning least-privilege IAM roles to developers is AWS best practice; long-lived IAM access keys (C) are a credential-leak risk and are not an access control solution for sensitive data.
saa-0920.aiExplanation: Option B is correct: define IAM roles with fine-grained, least-privilege permissions and have each developer assume the role that matches their job (typically through IAM Identity Center or role assumption), so they receive short-lived temporary credentials. This directly limits what each developer can reach and prevents unauthorized access to sensitive data. Option C relies on long-term IAM access keys, which AWS explicitly discourages because they can leak and never expire on their own, and access keys by themselves do not define any permissions. Option A shares credentials, which destroys accountability and violates basic security practice. Option D is wrong because Amazon Cognito user pools are for end users of applications, not for workforce access to AWS resources.

saa-0921.note: I believe B and E. To scale horizontally with an Auto Scaling group you need an AMI and a launch template (B) plus an ASG behind an ALB (E); a vertical-scaling recommendation (A) does not improve availability and an ASG with an ALB is a horizontal construct.
saa-0921.aiExplanation: The fix for a single overloaded instance that also needs better availability is horizontal scaling. First create an AMI from the existing web server and reference it in a launch template (B), which is the building block an Auto Scaling group needs to launch identical instances. Then create an Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones behind an Application Load Balancer (E) so capacity grows with demand and the app survives an instance or AZ failure. Option A only resizes one instance vertically, which still leaves a single point of failure and does not improve availability. Options C and D are internally inconsistent: an ASG with an ALB scales horizontally, not vertically, and Compute Optimizer recommends instance types, it does not perform horizontal scaling.

saa-0924.note: I believe B. Running steady-state tasks on Fargate and burst tasks on Fargate Spot in a capacity provider strategy is the standard cost-optimized, highly available pattern; D only rightsizes and does nothing to handle bursts cheaply.
saa-0924.aiExplanation: Option B uses an ECS capacity provider strategy with a base of regular Fargate tasks that always serve the 24/7 workload, and adds Fargate Spot tasks for short bursts. The baseline stays highly available because it never depends on Spot, while burst capacity costs up to about 70 percent less; if some Spot tasks are reclaimed during a burst the steady-state tasks keep serving customers. Option C reverses this and puts the always-on workload on interruptible Spot capacity, which risks availability. Options A and D only rightsize the task size; rightsizing is useful but does not address cost-effective handling of burst traffic, and A adds third-party load testing effort.

saa-0926.note: I believe B. AWS Shield Advanced protects against DDoS, not against unauthorized access attempts; NLBs support security groups, but they must be added when the NLB is created, so recreating the NLB with a security group that allows only trusted IPs is the minimal fix.
saa-0926.aiExplanation: Network Load Balancers now support security groups, which let you allow only trusted source IP ranges and block everything else at the load balancer. A security group can only be associated with an NLB at creation time, so the NLB must be recreated with one (B); this is a small architectural change and directly stops unauthorized clients. Option A is wrong because AWS WAF cannot be attached to an NLB, only to ALB, CloudFront, API Gateway, AppSync and similar layer 7 services. Option C adds a second load balancer and complexity without protecting the existing one. Option D, Shield Advanced, mitigates DDoS volumetric attacks but does not filter out individual unauthorized access attempts.

saa-0928.note: The keyed answer C is debatable: running an infrequent, on-demand extract program continuously in an Auto Scaling group with a Savings Plan is not very cost-effective, but it is the only option that truly requires no code changes. Option A (Lambda) is cheaper but would likely require repackaging the program and wiring an upload trigger.
saa-0928.aiExplanation: The deciding constraint is that the company does not want any code changes and wants the least implementation effort. Option C keeps both the web portal and the document extract program as they are, runs them in an Auto Scaling group for scalability and uptime, and lowers cost with a Savings Plan, so nothing needs to be rewritten. Option A would be cheaper for an infrequent job, but moving the extract program to AWS Lambda and invoking it on upload generally requires code and integration changes. Option B uses Spot Instances for a portal that requires 100 percent uptime, which is risky. Option D re-architects the portal onto S3, API Gateway and Lambda, which is a large code change.

saa-0929.note: I believe A and C. Cross-account SNS to Lambda needs a Lambda resource-based policy that lets SNS invoke the function and an SNS topic policy that lets the administrator account subscribe; adding an SQS buffer (B) is not required and would itself still need the cross-account topic permission.
saa-0929.aiExplanation: To have an SNS topic in one account trigger a Lambda function in another, two permissions are needed. The Lambda function's resource-based policy must allow the sns.amazonaws.com principal (scoped to the topic ARN) to invoke it (A). The SNS topic's access policy must allow the administrator account to subscribe its Lambda endpoint to the topic (C), after which the subscription is created. Option B adds an SQS queue, which is optional buffering and does not remove the need for the cross-account topic permission, so it does not complete the solution. Option D is wrong because EventBridge does not capture SNS message contents as events this way, and option E replaces the event-driven requirement with batch analysis in Athena.

saa-0940.note: The key (C, SSE-KMS with the AWS managed key) is defensible because AWS managed keys are free and rotate every year automatically, while a customer managed key costs a monthly fee. Double-check that you are comfortable with the claim that rotation of AWS managed keys is trackable in CloudTrail, which is why some argue for D.
saa-0940.aiExplanation: SSE-KMS with the AWS managed key for S3 (aws/s3) encrypts objects at rest, has no monthly key storage charge, and AWS rotates AWS managed keys automatically every year. Every use of the key is logged in AWS CloudTrail, which satisfies the tracking requirement at the lowest cost. A customer managed KMS key (D) also supports yearly automatic rotation with CloudTrail events, but costs about 1 USD per key per month, so it is not the cheapest. SSE-S3 (B) uses keys that are invisible to you and not trackable in CloudTrail, and SSE-C (A) makes you manage and rotate keys yourself.

saa-0950.note: The key C (existing bucket, CRR, SSE-S3, Athena) is the least-effort option, but note that CRR only replicates objects written after the rule is created, so existing data needs S3 Batch Replication; A avoids this by loading data into a new bucket after CRR is configured, at the cost of more setup.
saa-0950.aiExplanation: Amazon Athena is the serverless SQL engine for data in S3, which rules out B and D because Amazon RDS is not a serverless query layer over S3. Between A and C, C reuses the existing bucket, turns on Cross-Region Replication and uses SSE-S3, which is enabled by default and needs no key management, so it has the least operational overhead. The catch is that a new replication rule only applies to new objects; existing objects must be replicated once with S3 Batch Replication. Option A creates a new bucket with KMS multi-Region keys and reloads all the data, which works but adds key management and data movement effort.

saa-0951.note: The key A puts uploaded images in S3 Glacier Deep Archive because they are only read twice a year for training; this is defensible on cost, but debatable because the uploaded images are also used to generate AI images, and Deep Archive restores take up to 12 to 48 hours.
saa-0951.aiExplanation: Option A matches each data set to its access pattern. Uploaded images are only needed for model training twice a year, so S3 Glacier Deep Archive is the cheapest storage and a bulk restore before each training run is acceptable. Premium users can download generated images at any time, so S3 Standard fits, while non-premium users download at most once every 6 hours, so S3 Standard-IA is cheaper. Option C keeps uploaded images in One Zone-IA, which costs more than Deep Archive for data read twice a year and risks loss in an AZ failure. Options B and D put all generated images in Glacier Flexible Retrieval, which is too slow for premium users who need immediate downloads.

saa-0971.note: I believe A, C and E. Security groups are stateful and health checks are initiated by the ALB, so the ALB security group needs outbound rules to the instances on 443 and 8443; an inbound rule from the instances on 8443 (F) is never used.
saa-0971.aiExplanation: The ALB security group needs one inbound rule and two outbound rules. Inbound, it must allow HTTPS on port 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 so clients on the internet can reach it (A). Outbound, it must allow HTTPS to the web application instances on port 443 for forwarded traffic (C) and on port 8443 for the HTTPS health checks (E). Because security groups are stateful, return traffic is automatically allowed, so no inbound rules from the instances are needed; this rules out D and F. Option B is broader than necessary since it opens port 443 to the whole internet instead of only to the instances.

saa-0973.note: I believe A. Amazon Athena supports querying objects encrypted with CSE-KMS (set has_encrypted_data in the table properties), and it is the cheapest choice for occasional queries on day-partitioned Parquet; the key's claim that Athena cannot read CSE-KMS data is incorrect.
saa-0973.aiExplanation: Athena reads data in place in S3 and charges only for data scanned, which suits occasional queries, and Parquet plus per-day prefixes (partitions) keeps the scanned amount small. Athena supports the SSE-S3, SSE-KMS and CSE-KMS encryption options; for CSE-KMS you mark the table with has_encrypted_data and Athena decrypts using the KMS key. EMR Serverless with Spark SQL (D) can also read the data but needs job setup and has higher per-run overhead, so it is less cost-effective for ad hoc SQL. S3 Select (B) cannot query client-side encrypted objects and works on one object at a time, and Redshift Spectrum (C) requires a Redshift cluster or workgroup, which is unnecessary cost.

saa-0978.note: The answer C depends on a condition key that is missing from the question text (likely aws:ResourceAccount); without it the option is incomplete, so double-check the original wording.
saa-0978.aiExplanation: Option C adds a gateway VPC endpoint for S3 so traffic stays on the AWS network at no extra cost, and adds a Deny statement in the instance profile policy with a condition such as aws:ResourceAccount not equal to the company's account ID. This one statement covers every current and future customer bucket in the account, so nothing has to change as new buckets are added. Option A lists specific buckets, which must be updated every time a customer bucket is created, so it has more overhead. Options B and D route S3 traffic through a NAT gateway, which costs more and sends traffic over the public S3 endpoint, and D requires editing every bucket policy.

saa-0980.note: I believe B. IAM Roles Anywhere is designed to give on-premises workloads temporary AWS credentials using X.509 certificates; D still uses a long-term IAM user access key, which does not meet the temporary access requirement.
saa-0980.aiExplanation: IAM Roles Anywhere lets workloads outside AWS, such as on-premises virtual machines, exchange an X.509 certificate from a trusted certificate authority for temporary credentials of an IAM role, which can be scoped to only the required S3 bucket. This provides exactly the temporary, secure access the application needs and fits alongside the company's IAM Identity Center setup. Option D stores a long-term IAM user access key in Secrets Manager, which protects the key at rest but is still permanent credentials, not temporary access. Option C hardcodes IAM user keys in the CLI configuration, which is worse. Option A uses an IP-based bucket policy, which is weak and depends on a public path to S3.

saa-1004.note: I believe A and C. The AWSEC2-PatchLoadBalancerInstance runbook deregisters and re-registers instance targets, so the target group must use the instance target type; Maintenance Windows (D) only schedule tasks and do not by themselves remove instances from the load balancer.
saa-1004.aiExplanation: The errors come from trying to take instances out of service through a target group that registers targets by IP address. The AWSEC2-PatchLoadBalancerInstance Automation runbook (C) is built to deregister an EC2 instance from its load balancer target group, patch it, and register it back, and it works with instance-type targets, so changing the target group to the instance target type (A) removes the incompatibility. Option D is wrong because a Maintenance Window is only a schedule; it does not deregister instances from an ALB unless you run a runbook such as the one in C. Option B ignores the error, and option E misuses State Manager, which enforces configuration rather than draining instances from a load balancer.

saa-1006.note: I believe D. An Auto Scaling group with Spot capacity behind an ALB is the only option that scales seamlessly, and a stateless, resilient app tolerates Spot interruptions; A adds just one fixed instance and does not scale.
saa-1006.aiExplanation: The requirement is to make the application scale seamlessly at the lowest cost. Option D bakes the app into an AMI and launch template, runs it in an Auto Scaling group that adds and removes instances with demand, and puts an Application Load Balancer in front. Using Spot capacity is the cheapest compute, and because the application is stateless and highly resilient, losing an individual Spot instance only shifts traffic to the others. Option A only adds a second On-Demand instance, which is a fixed capacity that does not scale. Option B has the same problem and uses DNS weighting instead of load balancing, and option C stops the instance to resize it, causing downtime.

saa-1011.note: The keyed answer relies on Scheduled Reserved Instances, which AWS no longer offers for purchase; it is the intended exam answer, but in real life you would use On-Demand Capacity Reservations or simply cover the near-continuous usage with Reserved Instances or Savings Plans.
saa-1011.aiExplanation: The Sunday workload runs for a fixed 12-hour window and cannot be interrupted, which rules out Spot Instances in options C and D. Scheduled Reserved Instances were designed for exactly this kind of recurring, predictable time window at a discount, and Standard Reserved Instances give the biggest discount for instances that run constantly Monday to Saturday, which makes A the intended answer. Option B buys Convertible Reserved Instances for a 12-hour weekly window, so you would pay for a full-time reservation that is idle most of the week. Be aware that AWS stopped selling Scheduled Reserved Instances, so on a current account a Savings Plan or Reserved Instances covering the whole week are the realistic choice.

saa-1015.note: As written, D gives the UI pods access to S3 and the data service pods access to DynamoDB, which is the reverse of the requirement, so I believe C. D is very likely the intended answer with a typo, because IRSA with one role per service account is the correct mechanism.
saa-1015.aiExplanation: The right pattern is IAM roles for service accounts (IRSA): create a separate Kubernetes service account for the UI pods and for the data service pods, and map each to its own IAM role through the cluster's OIDC provider. Option C does this and gives the UI service account DynamoDB permissions and the data services account S3 permissions, which matches the requirement, although scoped-down policies would be better than the FullAccess managed policies. Option D uses the same mechanism but, as worded, grants UI pods S3 and data pods DynamoDB, the opposite of what is asked. Option A attaches both policies to the node instance profile, so every pod gets both permissions and Kubernetes RBAC cannot restrict AWS API access. Option B is not possible because IAM policies cannot be attached directly to pods.
